Flex layout disables the action button's right float

`.small-action` is now a flex container, so its direct `button` child is a flex item. Per the flexbox layout rules, the existing `float: right` on that item computes to `none`; without `margin-left: auto`, `justify-content`, or another positioning rule, the button is laid out immediately after `.small-action-desc` instead of at the right edge. This regresses the placement of small-action controls and can push them off the row when the description is wide. Add an explicit flex alignment rule (for example `margin-left: auto` on the button, with appropriate shrinking/growth for the description).

The flex alignment mixin omits the Mozilla legacy box property

`flexbox()` and `inline-flex()` deliberately emit `-moz-box` / `-moz-inline-box`, but `align-items()` does not emit the corresponding `-moz-box-align`. Firefox versions using the legacy box implementation will therefore ignore every `@include align-items(...)` call and use the legacy default alignment (stretch), including the newly centered header contents and baseline-aligned bullet badges. true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

The website_name inclusion predicate is not named according to serializer convention

Serializer conditional methods in this class use the `include_<attribute>?` form (for example, `include_email?` and `include_card_image_badge?`). This method is named `include_website_name` without the trailing `?`, so the serializer will not invoke it as the condition for `:website_name`; profiles without a website can therefore receive a `website_name: null` field instead of omitting it as intended. Rename it to `include_website_name?` and apply the same visibility condition as `website`.

Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue regarding string literal mutation (`'.' << website_host`), the candidate successfully catches the main functional bug.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the existing anonymous TL0 privacy restriction

`website` is explicitly listed in `untrusted_attributes`, so an anonymous viewer of a TL0 profile does not receive it. The newly added `website_name` attribute is not subject to that restriction, but is derived directly from the hidden website and can include both its host and path. As a result, anonymous clients receive profile URL information that the serializer intentionally withholds (for example, `example.com/private-profile`) even though `website` itself is absent. Add `website_name` to the same conditional visibility policy as `website` (and ensure its include predicate follows that policy).

Sibling hostnames are treated as the same domain using an unsafe label-count heuristic

For any two hostnames with more than two labels, this compares everything except the first label. That incorrectly treats unrelated registrable domains under multi-part public suffixes as the same domain: with an instance at `forum.github.io`, a website at `alice.github.io/private` will display `alice.github.io/private`, despite being a different site; the same occurs for hosts under `co.uk` and other public suffixes. The decision to expose the full path should use a public-suffix-aware registrable-domain comparison (or restrict it to exact hostname/known instance-domain relationships), rather than dropping the first DNS label.

Imported feed HTML is stored and served without sanitization

`import` creates posts with `cook_method: :raw_html` and `Post#cook` returns that raw HTML unchanged. Feed items are passed directly to this method by `PollFeed`, so a `<script>`, event handler, iframe, or other active markup in an RSS/Atom item is persisted and rendered with `raw post.cooked` in the embed and normal topic views. A compromised feed or untrusted content included by a feed can therefore execute JavaScript under the Discourse origin, including in an administrator's session. Sanitize imported HTML with the normal allowlist/cooking pipeline (or a strict dedicated sanitizer) before storing it, rather than bypassing cooking.

Direct article retrieval does not load open-uri before calling open

`import_remote` calls `open(url)` but this file does not require `open-uri`. The only new `require 'open-uri'` is in `Jobs::PollFeed`, which is not loaded on the normal embed retrieval path when feed polling is disabled. In a normal process where nothing else happened to load it, Kernel#open treats the HTTP URL as a file path and raises `Errno::ENOENT`, so requested embeds can never be imported. Require `open-uri` in this dependency's own file (or use an explicit HTTP client).

Remote retrieval follows redirects without validating the final destination

The host check in `TopicRetriever` only validates the original embed URL, but `open(url)` follows HTTP redirects. An allowed embed host with an open redirect (or a compromised allowed host) can redirect the worker to localhost, cloud metadata addresses, or other internal services; their response is then imported into a public topic. The expectation is therefore unsatisfied and the added controller spec fails whenever it runs. The work queues are unbounded, so slow processing provides no backpressure

`queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`, and `submit` uses a non-blocking-in-practice unbounded `put`. Therefore the Kafka strategy can continue polling and enqueueing indefinitely while one or more result processors are slow or unavailable. The stated natural backpressure never occurs; memory usage grows with the Kafka backlog and can OOM the consumer during a downstream outage. Use a bounded queue and make submission block or otherwise integrate its capacity with the processing strategy's backpressure mechanism.

Use a sentinel-based shutdown or a compatibility mechanism unless the project runtime is explicitly Python 3.13+.

The advertised graceful shutdown abandons queued work and stops commits before in-flight work finishes

`shutdown` immediately sets every worker's `shutdown` flag, so each worker exits after at most its currently active item rather than draining its queue. In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close`, the commit thread is stopped before this worker shutdown, so even an item that finishes during shutdown is not recorded as committed. A normal processor close can therefore abandon queued messages and replay already-processed in-flight messages after restart. Drain workers first (or explicitly terminate), then perform a final offset commit before stopping the commit loop.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context

The goroutine derives its timeout context from the request context. Once the API handler returns its successful unified-storage response, Kubernetes/Grafana can cancel that request context, which immediately cancels the legacy Create call (and the same pattern is used for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection). Consequently, many or all best-effort legacy writes can be aborted before they run, especially under normal request teardown. Derive the async context from a cancellation-detached context (while preserving required values) and apply the 10-second timeout to that context.

Independent async goroutines can apply legacy mutations out of order

Each successful unified write launches an independent goroutine, with no per-resource serialization or ordering. For example, a create followed immediately by an update or delete can execute in legacy as update/delete before create, or create after delete, leaving legacy with a stale or incorrect object even though unified storage is correct. Since mode 3 is intended to retain legacy as a safe copy, writes need an ordered queue/worker mechanism (at least per resource) rather than unconstrained concurrent goroutines.

Legacy update recomputes the update instead of mirroring the unified result

The legacy async call receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo after Storage.Update has completed. UpdatedObjectInfo is evaluated against the store's current/old object, so evaluating it again against potentially stale legacy state can generate a different payload, apply a stale resource version, or fail differently. The previous implementation explicitly evaluated the update and wrapped the unified result before passing it to legacy, ensuring both stores received the same object. Preserve that behavior by passing a wrapper containing the successful unified result to the legacy write.

Legacy outages can create an unbounded number of blocked goroutines

Every successful write creates a new goroutine that may remain blocked for up to ten seconds (or longer if a legacy implementation does not honor context cancellation). There is no queue capacity, worker limit, or backpressure. During a legacy outage and sustained write traffic this grows goroutine count and outstanding requests proportionally to traffic, risking memory exhaustion and scheduler degradation in the API server. Use bounded workers/queueing and define an overflow policy.

Mode 3 tests do not actually verify asynchronous legacy mirroring

Both the legacy and unified mock wrappers share one mock and use the same method names and argument matchers. For example, the legacy Create expectation at line 31 also matches the unified Storage.Create invocation, so the tests cannot identify which backend was called; the storage-failure case similarly configures only a purported legacy expectation. The tests also neither wait for the goroutine nor assert mock expectations. As a result, they pass without proving that legacy writes happen asynchronously, are skipped after unified failure, or receive the expected payload. Use separate mocks (or backend-identifying expectations), synchronize completion, and assert expectations.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Match-count updates lose increments under concurrent validation

The counter is updated with a read-modify-write sequence (`record.match_count += 1` followed by `save`). Two concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked address can both read the same count and save the same incremented value, causing one or more matches to be lost. Since this table explicitly records match statistics, use an atomic database update such as `update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')` or locking/counter updates so concurrent attempts are counted correctly.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment's main concern is the side effect inside a check method, with race conditions mentioned as a consequence. The candidate looks at the same code, the stats update in should_block_email?, and calls out the race condition from the non-atomic increment. That is partial overlap: same location, and race conditions are named in both. However, the candidate does not mention the misleading method name or the side effect during a read. It is likely still a match on the same underlying code issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-address matching is case-sensitive and can be trivially bypassed

`should_block?` compares the submitted value directly against the stored string. The signup path assigns `params[:email]` directly to `User#email`, so a row for `bad@spamclub.com` does not match a signup using `bad@SPAMCLUB.COM` (or other casing variants) on a case-sensitive database. This differs from the domain restrictions, which use a case-insensitive regexp, and allows a blocked address to register simply by changing case. Normalize both blocked-email records and values being checked with the application's canonical email normalization (for example `Email.downcase(...).strip`), and ensure lookup/indexing uses that normalized form.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same flaw: should_block? compares emails case-sensitively, so a blocked address can get through by changing its letter case.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Flex layout disables the action button's right float

`.small-action` is now a flex container, so its direct `button` child is a flex item. Per the flexbox layout rules, the existing `float: right` on that item computes to `none`; without `margin-left: auto`, `justify-content`, or another positioning rule, the button is laid out immediately after `.small-action-desc` instead of at the right edge. This regresses the placement of small-action controls and can push them off the row when the description is wide. Add an explicit flex alignment rule (for example `margin-left: auto` on the button, with appropriate shrinking/growth for the description).

The flex alignment mixin omits the Mozilla legacy box property

`flexbox()` and `inline-flex()` deliberately emit `-moz-box` / `-moz-inline-box`, but `align-items()` does not emit the corresponding `-moz-box-align`. Firefox versions using the legacy box implementation will therefore ignore every `@include align-items(...)` call and use the legacy default alignment (stretch), including the newly centered header contents and baseline-aligned bullet badges. Add `-moz-box-align: $alignment` alongside the other legacy declarations, or remove the unsupported legacy display mode if that browser family is no longer supported.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The website_name inclusion predicate is not named according to serializer convention

Serializer conditional methods in this class use the `include_<attribute>?` form (for example, `include_email?` and `include_card_image_badge?`). This method is named `include_website_name` without the trailing `?`, so the serializer will not invoke it as the condition for `:website_name`; profiles without a website can therefore receive a `website_name: null` field instead of omitting it as intended. Rename it to `include_website_name?` and apply the same visibility condition as `website`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same main issue as the golden comment: the include_website_name method is missing its ? suffix and so does not work as a conditional. It does not mention the string concatenation point, but the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the existing anonymous TL0 privacy restriction

`website` is explicitly listed in `untrusted_attributes`, so an anonymous viewer of a TL0 profile does not receive it. The newly added `website_name` attribute is not subject to that restriction, but is derived directly from the hidden website and can include both its host and path. As a result, anonymous clients receive profile URL information that the serializer intentionally withholds (for example, `example.com/private-profile`) even though `website` itself is absent. Add `website_name` to the same conditional visibility policy as `website` (and ensure its include predicate follows that policy).

Sibling hostnames are treated as the same domain using an unsafe label-count heuristic

For any two hostnames with more than two labels, this compares everything except the first label. That incorrectly treats unrelated registrable domains under multi-part public suffixes as the same domain: with an instance at `forum.github.io`, a website at `alice.github.io/private` will display `alice.github.io/private`, despite being a different site; the same occurs for hosts under `co.uk` and other public suffixes. The decision to expose the full path should use a public-suffix-aware registrable-domain comparison (or restrict it to exact hostname/known instance-domain relationships), rather than dropping the first DNS label.

Imported feed HTML is stored and served without sanitization

`import` creates posts with `cook_method: :raw_html` and `Post#cook` returns that raw HTML unchanged. Feed items are passed directly to this method by `PollFeed`, so a `<script>`, event handler, iframe, or other active markup in an RSS/Atom item is persisted and rendered with `raw post.cooked` in the embed and normal topic views. A compromised feed or untrusted content included by a feed can therefore execute JavaScript under the Discourse origin, including in an administrator's session. Sanitize imported HTML with the normal allowlist/cooking pipeline (or a strict dedicated sanitizer) before storing it, rather than bypassing cooking.

Direct article retrieval does not load open-uri before calling open

`import_remote` calls `open(url)` but this file does not require `open-uri`. The only new `require 'open-uri'` is in `Jobs::PollFeed`, which is not loaded on the normal embed retrieval path when feed polling is disabled. In a normal process where nothing else happened to load it, Kernel#open treats the HTTP URL as a file path and raises `Errno::ENOENT`, so requested embeds can never be imported. Require `open-uri` in this dependency's own file (or use an explicit HTTP client).

Remote retrieval follows redirects without validating the final destination

The host check in `TopicRetriever` only validates the original embed URL, but `open(url)` follows HTTP redirects. An allowed embed host with an open redirect (or a compromised allowed host) can redirect the worker to localhost, cloud metadata addresses, or other internal services; their response is then imported into a public topic. Validate every redirect target against an allowlist and block private/reserved IP ranges, or disable redirects and fetch only the validated origin.

Controller success spec expects a synchronous retriever that the controller never invokes

This example sets an expectation on `TopicRetriever.new` and `retrieve`, but `EmbedController#best` enqueues `:retrieve_topic` instead of constructing a `TopicRetriever`. The expectation is therefore unsatisfied and the added controller spec fails whenever it runs. Update the test to assert the `Jobs.enqueue` call (and cover execution in the retrieve-job spec), or change the implementation if synchronous retrieval was intended.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The new overload replaces the existing four-dimension downsize API

Ruby does not overload methods by arity. Defining `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` here replaces the preceding `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` definition, rather than adding a second accepted signature. Any existing caller using the formerly supported width/height form will now raise `ArgumentError` (five arguments supplied to a method accepting three or four), breaking thumbnail/image-processing callers outside this diff.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: the second downsize definition, which takes a single dimensions string, overrides the earlier one that took separate max_width and max_height. That makes the original unreachable and breaks existing callers that pass width and height separately.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side validation now ignores both configured image and attachment limits

Replacing `max_<type>_size_kb` with a hard-coded 10 MiB limit means attachments are now accepted by the browser even when `max_attachment_size_kb` is much smaller, only to fail on the server later. It also prevents clients from uploading images above 10 MiB when an administrator has configured a larger image limit. The larger pre-processing allowance should be limited to images that can actually be downsized; attachments must continue to use their configured limit.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the hardcoded 10MB limit ignores the per-type max_<type>_size_kb site settings, so the client-side limit diverges from the server-side one. The candidate does not mention the 413 handler, but the core issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Five fixed 80% reductions cannot ensure the upload meets the configured maximum

The reduction loop is capped at five iterations and each iteration only reduces dimensions to 80%, so a 10 MiB image is still roughly 3.3 MiB after all five attempts (and may compress even less effectively depending on image contents). Sites configured with a lower `max_image_size_kb` will still have the upload rejected by `Upload.create_for`, despite this path claiming to automatically reduce images to the allowed size. The resize ratio/iteration strategy needs to be based on the configured target or continue until the target is reached with a safe termination condition.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Manual unsubscribe URLs fail with a nil TopicUser record

`TopicUser.find_by` can return nil when a logged-in user visits an unsubscribe URL for a topic they have not previously viewed or otherwise received a topic-user row for. The following access to `tu.notification_level` then raises a 500 error. The route is publicly reachable and the new client route makes such navigation possible, so the action must create/update the association via `TopicUser.change` or handle a missing record before reading it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out that TopicUser.find_by can return nil and that calling methods on tu, such as notification_level, will then crash. It is the same nil pointer issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsubscribe bypasses TopicUser.change and can be undone by auto-tracking

The action writes `notification_level` directly and leaves `notifications_reason_id` nil for topic-user records created by ordinary visits. `TopicUser.update_last_read` treats a nil reason as eligible for automatic promotion to `tracking`; therefore, after this endpoint mutes such a topic, a later read that crosses the auto-track threshold can silently change it back to tracking and resume topic email notifications. Use the notification-state update path (or explicitly persist a user-changed reason and timestamp) rather than directly saving the record. The direct save also omits the MessageBus notification used to synchronize other open clients.

A GET request changes a user's notification preference

`unsubscribe` mutates `TopicUser.notification_level` in response to a GET request, and the action is explicitly exempted from the XHR check. Any site can cause a logged-in user's browser to request a known public topic unsubscribe URL (for example with an image or redirect), changing that user's per-topic notification state without consent. State changes should require a CSRF-protected non-GET request, with the email link leading to a confirmation page or a signed one-time action token.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook helper cannot update env files on GNU/Linux sed

On GNU sed, commonly used on Linux development environments and CI, the separate empty argument is not handled as the intended backup suffix and the command fails rather than updating `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL`. Use a portable conditional for BSD versus GNU sed, or rewrite the file without relying on platform-specific `sed -i` behavior.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the macOS/BSD `sed -i ''` syntax fails on Linux GNU sed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is formatted with a hard-coded US locale

The component uses `Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US")` even though its surrounding labels are localized through `useLocale`. Users with non-US locales will always receive US date ordering and formatting for the cache status, which conflicts with the localized UI. Format using the active application/user locale instead of a literal `en-US`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the date is formatted with a hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of the user's locale from useLocale.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting cache does not invalidate the connected-calendars query

The delete-cache mutation only calls the optional `onSuccess` callback. Unlike the disconnect mutation below it, it never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, which is the query supplying `cacheUpdatedAt`. When this component is used without a callback that explicitly refetches that query, a successful deletion leaves the UI showing the old cache timestamp and the delete action until a manual reload. Invalidate the connected-calendars query on mutation settlement/success (and optionally integrations if needed).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fixed-host override validation accepts slots that extend outside the override

The override check only rejects a slot when it ends at/before the override start or starts strictly after the override end. A slot that starts inside the override but ends after it, or starts exactly at the override end, falls through and is treated as available. For example, with a fixed host override of 10:00-11:00 and a 60-minute event, an 10:30 or 11:00 slot can be returned for a round-robin event even though the fixed host is unavailable for part or all of it. The check must require the entire slot to be within the override interval, including rejecting equality at the end boundary.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment says the end-boundary check uses slotStartTime where it should use slotEndTime. The candidate describes the resulting bug: a slot that starts inside the override but ends after it is accepted, because the check only compares the slot's start to the override end. Both point to the same flawed comparison.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Empty date overrides are compared by object identity and do not block their start slot

`dayjs(...) === dayjs(...)` compares two distinct Dayjs objects by reference, so this condition is always false even when `date.start` and `date.end` represent the same instant. Empty/zero-length date overrides (used to represent no availability) therefore fall through; the slot beginning exactly at that instant is considered available because neither subsequent strict boundary check matches it. Compare the instants with `isSame` (or timestamps) and reject the override date as unavailable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: dayjs objects compared with ===, which checks reference equality and so is always false. Both recommend using isSame instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Override selection ignores timezone-driven date changes

Overrides are selected by comparing the unadjusted UTC-encoded `override.start` date to the invitee day, but their times are subsequently shifted by the organizer/invitee offset. When that shift crosses midnight, the override is applied to a different invitee calendar day than the one used by this filter, so it is omitted entirely. For example, an early-morning Asia/Kolkata override can correspond to the prior calendar day for an America/New_York attendee; requesting that attendee day will return regular availability instead of the override. Filter based on the override interval after converting it to the invitee timezone (and account for intervals overlapping the day).

Working-hours validation rejects valid slots for split schedules

The code uses `workingHours.find` to find any working-hours interval that does not contain the slot, rather than confirming that at least one interval contains it. With a normal split schedule such as 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00, a 14:00 slot is rejected as soon as the first interval is examined, even though it is valid in the second interval. This can hide otherwise bookable round-robin slots for fixed hosts. The validation should accept when any same-day interval fully contains the slot, and reject only when none do.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry count updates can lose increments when cron invocations overlap

The handler reads `reminder.retryCount` and writes `reminder.retryCount + 1` rather than using an atomic database increment. Two overlapping cron requests can both read 0, both fail scheduling, and both write 1; the reminder then survives another run despite two failed attempts. Overlapping invocations are also especially plausible while a reminder remains unscheduled. Use Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }` update (and consider claiming the reminder/conditional updates to avoid concurrent scheduling) so the deletion threshold reflects actual failures.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the code reads retryCount and writes retryCount + 1, which can lose increments when updates run concurrently. Both recommend Prisma's atomic increment as the fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry cleanup is not restricted to SMS reminders

The new `retryCount > 1` branch is a top-level OR condition with no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` restriction. Consequently, any EMAIL or WHATSAPP `WorkflowReminder` whose retryCount is greater than one will be permanently deleted by this SMS cron endpoint, even though this retry policy is intended only for SMS. Scope the retry-count predicate to SMS reminders (and, if appropriate, unscheduled reminders) so this job cannot remove reminders owned by other delivery paths.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the retryCount > 1 OR branch lacks a method: SMS filter, so the SMS cron job deletes Email and WhatsApp reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Reminders with no renderable message or recipient never consume retries

`retryCount` is only incremented after `scheduleSMS` returns false or throws. If `sendTo` is absent (possible because both the booking SMS number and workflow step recipient are optional) or message generation results in an empty value, this condition is skipped entirely. The reminder remains `scheduled: false` and is fetched on every cron run until its date passes, which leaves a common unsendable-SMS case unfixed by the retry cap. Treat an unusable recipient/message as a failed scheduling attempt, or delete/mark the reminder as unsendable.

Removing `findMany` breaks the exported service API

`findMany` was the service's data-access API and applied the authorization and filter predicates together with caller-provided `findMany` arguments. This change removes it and exposes only a raw SQL fragment, while no dependent call sites are migrated in this PR. Existing consumers of `InsightsBookingService.findMany` will fail to compile/run, and replacement callers must now independently choose the correct table/view and reimplement Prisma query features such as selection, ordering, pagination, and additional `where` clauses. Preserve a compatible query method or update all consumers as part of this change.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

The golden comment says this throws a runtime error. The candidate says the keys evaluate to "[object Object]" and cause fields to be stripped. The predicted consequences differ, but the underlying bug is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

Google refresh stores the Zod safe-parse wrapper as the credential key

The buffer still exposes `max_segment_spans` as a constructor option, but the only span-count enforcement is now hard-coded to 1000 in Lua. The previous flush-side limit used `self.max_segment_spans`; after this change custom deployments cannot lower or raise the limit, and segments between their configured limit and 1000 are emitted rather than rejected/limited as configured. Pass the configured limit to the script and enforce that value, or remove/document the option and update callers if a fixed 1000-span contract is intentional.

Redirect traversal limit is reduced and can split deep traces

The redirect-chain traversal limit is reduced from 10,000 to 1,000. For a trace whose buffered parent chain exceeds 1,000 links, the script stops resolving redirects and attaches the arriving span to an intermediate buffer rather than the root buffer. Those buffers can then be queued and flushed as separate segments, producing incorrect segment IDs and incomplete trace segments. Retain the prior limit or add a safe chain-compression strategy rather than silently reducing the supported tree depth.

false_negatives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses the outer dataset instead of the dataset actually queried

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset`, but eligibility is evaluated against the `dataset` captured from the original request. In the dashboard split path, an enhanced-metrics widget can call `_get_event_stats(discover, ..., errors_only_query, ...)` while the captured dataset is a metrics dataset. `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` rejects metrics datasets, so this explicitly error-only Discover subquery is never upsampled despite all projects being allowlisted. Evaluate eligibility against `scoped_dataset` and the actual `query` argument rather than the original request context.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: upsampling eligibility is evaluated against the outer/original dataset rather than the scoped dataset actually queried. It cites the same dashboard-split path where a Discover subquery is skipped because the captured dataset is metrics, despite allowlisted projects.

false_positives.candidate:
Raw substring check enables upsampling for non-error Discover queries

The Discover eligibility check treats any query containing the text `event.type:error` as error-only. This is not a semantic query check: for example, `!event.type:error` (a supported syntax used elsewhere in this endpoint) contains that substring but explicitly selects non-error events, and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` selects transactions as well. Those queries will be rewritten to sum `sample_weight`, even though transactions/non-error events do not have error sampling weights, producing failed queries or incorrect counts. Determine event-type constraints from the parsed query and require that the query cannot include non-error event types.

The internal upsampling aggregate is exposed to client queries

`upsampled_count` is registered without `private=True`, unlike the adjacent internal aggregate. As a result, clients can request `upsampled_count()` directly through Discover/Event Stats without passing the allowlist and event-type checks in `error_upsampling.py`. This permits unallowlisted or mixed-event queries to use `sample_weight`, yielding unsupported/incorrect results (or query failures where the field is unavailable). Mark the function private and expose it only through the guarded rewrite.

Upsampled counts truncate fractional sampling weights

The implementation applies `toInt64` to `sum(sample_weight)`. Sampling rates are floats (the added test factory explicitly converts `client_sample_rate` to float), so weights such as `1 / 0.3` and sums of heterogeneous weights are not necessarily integral. Casting the final sum to an integer truncates the estimate and systematically underreports error counts. Return the numeric sum directly, or use the established rounding behavior for sampled-count estimates if the API contract requires integral counts.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache key is ambiguous for UIDs containing underscores

The key concatenates `name` and `parent` with an unescaped underscore, so distinct resource/folder pairs can produce the same cache key (for example name `a_b` with parent `c`, and name `a` with parent `b_c`). Since dashboard and folder UIDs can contain underscores, a denial for one pair can incorrectly deny another pair for 30 seconds. Encode the fields unambiguously (for example length-prefixing or structured encoding) before using them in the cache key.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same cache-key collision caused by underscore concatenation of UID components, leading to incorrect permission denials. The candidate provides a concrete example and remediation but identifies the same underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial-cache hit prevents newly granted permissions from being observed

A denial entry is returned before consulting either the permission cache or the database, and there is no invalidation when a role, team membership, or resource permission is granted. Consequently, if a Check is denied just before or during creation of a dashboard/folder or an IAM permission update, subsequent checks for that exact resource remain denied for `shortCacheTTL` (30 seconds), even though the DB would now authorize them. This defeats the new stale-cache fallback for the case it is intended to solve. Either invalidate denial keys on permission/resource changes or do not use a denial entry to bypass the DB recheck for newly mutable permissions.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing integrations without webhook sender metadata cause a server error

The comparison indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`, but `build_integration` creates GitHub integrations without a `sender` field and all integrations created before this change also lack it. If such an Integration remains after its OrganizationIntegration is removed (or was created through the no-record branch above), a later installation attempt reaches this code and raises KeyError instead of returning the intended installation failure response. Treat missing or malformed sender metadata as an unverified request and return the error page (or migrate/populate the metadata) rather than indexing it directly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: direct indexing of integration.metadata['sender']['login'] raises KeyError when sender metadata is absent for existing or newly built integrations. The candidate describes the same failure mode and remediation.

false_positives.candidate:
New installations bypass the GitHub installer identity check

When no Integration row exists yet, this branch immediately advances to integration creation without checking the GitHub account that installed the app. This is a normal race because the browser redirect from GitHub can reach this pipeline before the installation webhook has created the Integration containing `metadata.sender`; `build_integration` only fetches installation details and does not establish the installing user. A user can start their own valid Sentry/OAuth pipeline and submit a newly created/known installation ID during that window, causing the installation to be linked to their Sentry organization even though their OAuth user is not the app installer. The identity check must be performed from trustworthy installation/user data before allowing this branch, or the flow must wait for/require the webhook record with a sender.

OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Register cleanup for the created IDP alias, not the literal "alias"

Each created provider is named `idp-alias-<i>`, but the cleanup callback is registered against `identityProviders().get("alias")`. The cleanup will therefore attempt to delete a non-existent provider and leave all providers created by this test behind (the same issue occurs for `idp-alias-20` at line 425). This can pollute the shared test realm and cause later tests or reruns to observe unexpected IDPs. Register cleanup using the actual alias created in each case.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: cleanup is registered against the literal alias "alias" instead of the actual created provider alias `idp-alias-<i>`, so cleanup deletes a non-existent provider and leaves test IDPs behind.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
No automated regression test verifies SQL expressions remain disabled

This security-sensitive behavior is implemented without accompanying tests. Add coverage that submits a QueryTypeSQL expression with FlagSqlExpressions both enabled and disabled and asserts that it is rejected, plus coverage for the legacy SQL command construction path if it remains reachable. Without this, a future refactor of the feature-toggle logic or command wiring can silently re-enable SQL execution and reintroduce the RCE/LFI exposure.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent cold-cache callers all reload the manifest serially

The cache is checked before acquiring the write lock, but it is not checked again after the lock is acquired. If several non-dev requests arrive while the cache is empty, each observes `nil`, waits for the previous caller to finish reading/parsing the manifest, and then performs its own file/CDN load while holding the exclusive lock. This turns one initialization load into one serialized load per concurrent request and blocks cache readers for the duration of each load. Recheck `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the lock (for non-dev mode) and return it if another goroutine populated it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same incomplete double-checked locking bug in GetWebAssets: the cache is checked before acquiring the write lock but not rechecked afterward, so concurrent cold-cache callers each perform redundant serialized loads. The candidate's suggested fix matches the golden concern.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors and dump every selected ID

Every batch logs at Error level before and after deletion even when `err` is nil, and includes the complete `ids` slice. A configured large batch (the added test uses 32,767 IDs) produces very large error log entries for normal operation, pollutes error monitoring, and can materially increase logging/storage load during cleanup. Log only actual errors at Error level and use a non-error level with counts rather than the full ID list for successful batches.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same problem: non-error/debug cleanup information is logged at Error level, polluting production error logs. The candidate adds specifics about full ID dumps and suggests counts at a non-error level, but the underlying concern matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup scheduling is changed from every ten minutes to every minute for all cleanup jobs

This unrelated change makes the entire cleanup suite run ten times as often, not just annotation cleanup. It increases database scans/deletes and filesystem work for snapshots, dashboard versions, images, short URLs, query history, and annotations, and can cause a long-running cleanup to be re-run immediately after it completes because the ticker has already fired. There is no corresponding configuration or PR rationale for this broad scheduling change; retain the ten-minute interval unless this load increase is explicitly intended and validated.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same change: the cleanup job interval was reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute, causing all cleanup tasks to run much more frequently and increasing database/filesystem load. The candidate adds detail but points to the same underlying concern.

false_positives.candidate:
The new per-ID delete can exceed supported parameter counts on non-SQLite databases

`deleteByIDs` creates one bound parameter for every selected ID except for SQLite. `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` is configurable and the added test explicitly exercises 32,767 IDs; this exceeds SQL Server's 2,100-parameter limit (and sufficiently large configured values can exceed limits on other supported dialects). The previous DELETE used no per-ID bind list, so such configurations worked. On those deployments cleanup will fail each batch and old annotations/tags will accumulate. Split the delete into dialect-safe chunks or apply the same safe literal/chunking strategy for every dialect with a parameter limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unified-storage failures are recorded as legacy durations

When Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration using the unified-storage timing even though no legacy write was attempted. The same error exists in Update at line 129, and DeleteCollection records the async legacy duration as storage duration at line 166. This makes backend/error metrics and alerts report the wrong failing system; use recordStorageDuration for unified operations and recordLegacyDuration for the async legacy operation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in DualWriterMode3.DeleteCollection where the wrong duration-recording function is used on failure, swapping storage vs legacy metrics. The candidate explicitly cites DeleteCollection line 166 and the recordStorageDuration/recordLegacyDuration mix-up, matching the golden issue despite broader scope.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete metric uses resource name as the kind label

The successful delete metric passes `name` where all other calls pass `options.Kind`. Object names are effectively unbounded and often user-controlled, so each deleted object creates a distinct Prometheus label value/time series that is never reclaimed by the metric vector. This can cause unbounded metric memory/cardinality growth. Pass `options.Kind` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the delete metric records the resource name rather than options.Kind, unlike other methods. The candidate additionally explains the resulting metric cardinality issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context

The goroutine derives its timeout context from the request context. Once the API handler returns its successful unified-storage response, Kubernetes/Grafana can cancel that request context, which immediately cancels the legacy Create call (and the same pattern is used for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection). Consequently, many or all best-effort legacy writes can be aborted before they run, especially under normal request teardown. Derive the async context from a cancellation-detached context (while preserving required values) and apply the 10-second timeout to that context.

Independent async goroutines can apply legacy mutations out of order

Each successful unified write launches an independent goroutine, with no per-resource serialization or ordering. For example, a create followed immediately by an update or delete can execute in legacy as update/delete before create, or create after delete, leaving legacy with a stale or incorrect object even though unified storage is correct. Since mode 3 is intended to retain legacy as a safe copy, writes need an ordered queue/worker mechanism (at least per resource) rather than unconstrained concurrent goroutines.

Legacy update recomputes the update instead of mirroring the unified result

The legacy async call receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo after Storage.Update has completed. UpdatedObjectInfo is evaluated against the store's current/old object, so evaluating it again against potentially stale legacy state can generate a different payload, apply a stale resource version, or fail differently. The previous implementation explicitly evaluated the update and wrapped the unified result before passing it to legacy, ensuring both stores received the same object. Preserve that behavior by passing a wrapper containing the successful unified result to the legacy write.

Legacy outages can create an unbounded number of blocked goroutines

Every successful write creates a new goroutine that may remain blocked for up to ten seconds (or longer if a legacy implementation does not honor context cancellation). There is no queue capacity, worker limit, or backpressure. During a legacy outage and sustained write traffic this grows goroutine count and outstanding requests proportionally to traffic, risking memory exhaustion and scheduler degradation in the API server. Use bounded workers/queueing and define an overflow policy.

Mode 3 tests do not actually verify asynchronous legacy mirroring

Both the legacy and unified mock wrappers share one mock and use the same method names and argument matchers. For example, the legacy Create expectation at line 31 also matches the unified Storage.Create invocation, so the tests cannot identify which backend was called; the storage-failure case similarly configures only a purported legacy expectation. The tests also neither wait for the goroutine nor assert mock expectations. As a result, they pass without proving that legacy writes happen asynchronously, are skipped after unified failure, or receive the expected payload. Use separate mocks (or backend-identifying expectations), synchronize completion, and assert expectations.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu action cannot open a drawer for Prometheus-only Grafana rules

The new list supplies only `promRule`, so `AlertRuleMenu` can expose “Silence notifications” based on `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` and clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true. However, the drawer is rendered only when a Ruler alerting rule is present (`rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`), which is false when `rule` is undefined. Consequently the menu item is visible and clickable but produces no UI or action in the alert list.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: for Grafana rules supplied only as promRule, the Silence notifications action sets showSilenceDrawer, but the drawer is gated on a Grafana Ruler rule and never renders, so the click has no effect.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete is unavailable for Grafana rules rendered without a Ruler payload

Although `canDelete` now includes the Grafana Prometheus-rule ability, the delete menu item still additionally requires `rulerRule`. `GrafanaRuleListItem` only passes a `promRule`, so users with delete permission never see Delete in the new Grafana alert list. The delete handler passed by `RuleActionsButtons` only needs the already computed identifier, so retaining this payload guard removes an existing rule-management operation.

Pause action is hidden for Prometheus-only Grafana list entries

`canPause` now correctly considers the Grafana Prometheus-rule ability, but rendering the pause item still requires a Grafana Ruler rule. Since the new list intentionally no longer loads or passes that Ruler rule, the pause/unpause operation disappears from the list even for editable Grafana-managed alerting rules. The pause action needs to be migrated to operate from the Prometheus representation/identifier or omitted from the advertised supported abilities.

Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable

The previous implementation determined federation from `rule.group` via `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. This replacement unconditionally sets `isFederated` to false, including when called through `useAllAlertRuleAbilities`, which still receives the complete `CombinedRule`. Federated datasource rules can therefore be presented as editable, deletable, pausable, or restorable when the prior behavior intentionally disabled those operations, risking invalid or unintended changes to federated rule groups.

Grafana rule view links no longer preserve the current list location

The removed `GrafanaRuleListItem` built its view URL with `createReturnTo()`, allowing the rule view to navigate back to the current filtered/paginated alert list. false_negatives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

false_positives.candidate:
Interpolating before the $__range split guard makes range-variable queries split incorrectly

`querySupportsSplitting` intentionally excludes expressions containing range variables because their value must correspond to the unsplit request range. This change applies template variables before that check, so an expression such as `rate({app="api"}[$__range])` becomes a literal duration before `isQueryWithRangeVariable` runs and is no longer recognized as exempt. It will then be split into daily requests while retaining the duration calculated from the original full range, producing incorrect query windows and potentially duplicated or missing metric results. Preserve the pre-interpolation range-variable decision (or carry that metadata through interpolation) before partitioning.

Queries that interpolate to an empty expression are no longer filtered out

The previous flow interpolated all targets and only then filtered out empty `expr` values. The new flow filters before `applyTemplateVariables`, so a target whose expression is a variable that resolves to an empty string is retained and passed into shard grouping and eventually query execution. This can send an invalid empty LogQL query instead of ignoring it; if it is the only target, it can also create a group where none should exist. Filter the interpolated `queries` collection for `query.expr` after mapping (and apply the same post-interpolation filtering in the time-splitting path).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert does not enforce the limit under concurrent requests

The limit check performs `CountDevices` in one database session and then performs the insert/upsert in a separate session. Multiple concurrent requests for distinct device IDs can all observe a count below `deviceLimit` and all insert successfully, exceeding the configured limit. This also occurs across Grafana instances sharing the same database. The check and admission need to be made atomic, for example with a transaction and suitable locking or a database-side conditional/admission mechanism.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition where concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic count check and insert devices beyond the limit. The candidate's recommendation for a transaction, locking, or database-side conditional admission matches the golden fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected devices are cached and allowed on their next request

`tagDeviceUI` adds the device ID to the local cache before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When that call returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, this new return rejects the current authentication, but the cache entry remains. A subsequent request from the same new device ID hits the cache and returns success without consulting the store, so `Authenticate` creates an anonymous identity despite the configured limit. Since the cache default TTL is 29 minutes, a device can bypass the limit simply by retrying after its first rejected request. Only cache the ID after a successful store update, or evict it when tagging fails.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrOther body, and an ErrDeviceLimitReached failure leaves the entry cached, allowing a retry to bypass the limit until the 29-minute TTL expires.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback translations are only loaded for controller requests

The lazy translation loader only loads the current locale during `I18n.translate`; a fallback lookup performed by `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` reads the fallback locale directly from the backend and does not invoke `I18n.translate` again. This callback preloads fallback locales only for requests that pass through `ApplicationController`. Mailers, background jobs, model/service code, and any other `I18n.t` call outside that controller will therefore load (for example) `fr` but not the configured site locale or `en`, so missing French strings still resolve as missing translations on a cold process. Fallback locale loading needs to happen as part of translation/fallback resolution rather than only in this controller filter.

Translation cache does not include the dynamic fallback chain

A no-options translation is cached only by key, current locale, and backend object. The new fallback result also depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, which can be changed at runtime, but this change adds no cache invalidation for that setting. After changing the site default locale, keys absent from a user's locale can continue returning the old default locale's cached text until the entry is evicted or I18n is reloaded, producing stale and inconsistent server-rendered translations.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin completion logs no longer include the trace ID

The previous implementation explicitly extracted `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` and appended it as the `traceID` structured log field. The new contextual logger middleware only adds endpoint/plugin/datasource/user fields, and this call now logs only `logParams` obtained from `FromContext`, so no trace ID is added. As a result, backend plugin request completion logs cannot be correlated with traces anymore, regressing the existing observability contract. Add the trace ID to the contextual attributes or retain it in `logParams`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same regression: refactoring removed traceID extraction from plugin request logging, and the new contextual logger does not add it, so completion logs can no longer be correlated with traces.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to the exported Logger interface breaks downstream implementations

`Logger` is an exported interface, and adding a required `FromContext(context.Context)` method means every existing custom implementation outside this change no longer satisfies it and will fail to compile when upgrading. This is a source-incompatible API change in addition to the middleware rename. Preserve compatibility by using a separate optional contextual-logger interface/type assertion at the call site, or provide an adapter/migration path rather than extending the existing interface.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when the legacy embed_category setting was never persisted

The migration unconditionally indexes the first row returned by the `embed_category` query (`...[0]['id']`). Site settings with their default value are not necessarily stored in `site_settings`, so a deployment that configured allowed hosts but left the category at its default has no `embed_category` row. In that common case `[0]` is nil and the migration aborts before it can fall back to Uncategorized. Handle an empty result before indexing it (and likewise make the fallback query robust).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same migration bug: unconditionally indexing the first row of the embed_category query crashes when no row exists because the default setting was never persisted.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy hosts are copied without normalization and stop matching requests

The old setting accepted values such as `http://discourse.org` and `https://example.com/path` (the existing tests explicitly cover those forms), but this migration inserts those strings verbatim. `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` subsequently extracts only the request hostname and compares it to the stored `host`, so a migrated row containing a scheme or path can never authorize that host. Existing embedding installations using those supported legacy formats will begin rejecting embeds and topic retrievals after migration. `forEach(async ...)` does not await its callbacks. Consequently the surrounding `try/catch` only covers scheduling the callbacks; an import failure or `deleteEvent` failure is not caught, and the reschedule flow continues to email/return before cleanup is complete. Since `getCalendar` now always introduces an await point, this is reliably asynchronous rather than merely an unawaited provider deletion. Collect and await the callback promises with `Promise.all`.

The candidate is more specific about forEach not awaiting callbacks and recommends Promise.all, but it identifies the same underlying import-failure handling issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
